title: Milk between
hookLine: from between waste and blood, pure milk, pleasant to drink (16:66)

lines: A GLASS OF MILK AT NIGHT.
cards: A glass of milk on a kitchen table at night. It's about the plainest thing in the house. It goes into tea, into coffee, into a child's cereal, and nobody asks where it was made.
An-Nahl has been listing gifts since its opening: rain, cattle, date palms, grapes, the stars you steer by.
In the middle of that list it stops at the plainest drink there is, points at the inside of an animal, and says: look where this came from.

teach.b: Pickthall translates 16:66 like this: "And lo! in the cattle there is a lesson for you."
Then: "We give you to drink of that which is in their bellies, from betwixt the refuse and the blood, pure milk palatable to the drinkers."

In Arabic, lesson is 'ibrah, from a root meaning to cross over: you look at one thing and arrive somewhere else. The verse wants you to cross from a glass of milk to the One who gave it. Now the picture.
It names two things nobody wants to drink, waste and blood, and between them, something you'd hand to a child. Two words describe it.

teach.h: KHALIS: PURE. SA'IGH: EASY TO DRINK.
teach.b: Khalis: pure, unmixed, sharing a root with ikhlas, sincerity, the name of Surah 112. And sa'igh: easy to swallow, going down without a struggle. The verse gives no lecture on how milk is made.
Classical commentators wrote about it with what they knew in their day; the verse only says: here is your drink. Milk mattered in the Prophet's life.

A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught that whoever is given milk should ask God to bless it for them and give them more of it, and said he knew nothing else that served as both food and drink.
So the verse lands on something people lived on, and hands you a way to see.
A lot of what's good in a life came out from between things you'd never choose: a friendship from a terrible job, patience from a long illness, a recipe from a lean year.
The verse doesn't say the waste and blood were good.

teach.h: PURE MILK PALATABLE TO THE DRINKERS.
teach.b: It says something pure came out from between them.

how: Muslims commonly say bismillah before eating or drinking and alhamdulillah after, and some follow the Prophet's teaching to ask for blessing when given milk; 16:66 is often cited when speaking of everyday gifts.

o: the milk of paradise, promised to flow in a river
milk set aside only for the sick and the very old
pure milk, brought out from between waste and blood

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: a lesson: something you cross over from
milk from between waste and blood

s: the verse explains exactly how milk is made
it names where milk comes from and calls it a lesson; it gives no mechanism.
khalis, pure, shares a root with ikhlas, sincerity
the same three letters, kh-l-s: pure, unmixed.
the Prophet taught a prayer of blessing for when you're given milk
Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi record it, with his words that milk served as food and drink.

games.q: you're handed a glass of milk at the end of a long day. the verse calls it a lesson. what does it ask you to look at?
o: where it came from: between waste and blood, yet pure.
games.why: the verse points at the inside of the animal: pure milk from between waste and blood. 'ibrah means crossing from what you see to the One who gave it.

practice: If there's a drink near you, hold it and think back along its road: the animal or the cloud, the field, the truck, the person who stocked the shelf.
Muslim custom is to say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after; if you pray, you can do the same. Take one slow sip, and notice how easily it goes down: that's the verse's word.

wordCard.voice: Milk between. Pure milk, easy to drink, brought out from between waste and blood: a lesson in the plainest drink in the house. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: pure milk (16:66). khalis shares the root kh-l-s with ikhlas, sincerity.

carryVoice: Your line: pure from between. The mess wasn't nice, and what came from it can still be good. Until tomorrow.
